article.title: Federal Prosecutors Charge Atlanta Man for Wiping His Phone With a GrapheneOS 'Duress Password' at the Airport
article.summary: US prosecutors are pursuing an Atlanta man under a rarely used federal statute after he allegedly used a GrapheneOS 'duress password' to wipe his phone during a border search.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Federal prosecutors are charging Atlanta resident Sam Tunick under a little-known statute that makes it a crime to destroy property to prevent its seizure, after agents say he wiped his phone during a search at the airport, according to [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/policy/971097/us-charging-american-citizen-wiping-phone-duress-password) and [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). Tunick was stopped at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on January 24, 2025, as he returned from a vacation in the Dominican Republic, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone).

## What We Know

Agents took Tunick to a room for a "secondary inspection," complete with a table, chairs, and a camera and microphone, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). During questioning that touched on child sexual abuse images, agents pressed him to unlock his phone. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/policy/971097/us-charging-american-citizen-wiping-phone-duress-password) reports that Tunick used a feature of GrapheneOS to give authorities a "duress password" instead of his actual passcode — a mechanism that wipes the device rather than unlocking it. According to the motion filed by Tunick's federal public defenders, as reported by [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone), when he finally provided a passcode, "the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart." Prosecutors are treating the wipe as intentional destruction of evidence, while the defense frames it as a consequence of the search itself rather than deliberate obstruction.

GrapheneOS is described by [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone) as "an open-source operating system that enables users to enter a passcode and wipe a phone clean," and by [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/policy/971097/us-charging-american-citizen-wiping-phone-duress-password) as "the privacy-focused GrapheneOS."

Tunick's federal public defenders argue in their motion that the prosecution is a pretext tied to his alleged ties to the movement against Atlanta's Cop City police training facility. According to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone), federal authorities had placed Tunick on a terrorism watchlist because of his alleged association with that movement, opposition to which came from a wide range of local and national organizations and protesters directed at the $109 million training center that opened last spring. The Guardian reports the motion describes the interrogation, including the child-sexual-abuse-images questions, as "a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick's connections" to the anti-Cop-City movement. The motion also states that Tunick "asked four times during the interrogation to speak with a lawyer, but was rebuffed each time," and that agents produced no warrant and did not read him his rights, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone).

Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, defended the use of privacy tools like GrapheneOS, telling [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/policy/971097/us-charging-american-citizen-wiping-phone-duress-password): "We all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism."

Christophe Boutry, a cybersecurity and surveillance expert, raised concerns about the precedent the case could set, telling [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone): "It's concerning – and sends the message that [GrapheneOS] is criminal by default." Boutry added that "the main goal [of the operating system] is protection of privacy," and said: "They're our phones and the state can't tell us how to use them."

The case had its first hearing on Monday, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone), and a judge's decision on the defense motion to suppress evidence is not expected until at least the end of October, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone).

## What We Don't Know

Neither outlet reporting on the case cites a specific statute number for the property-destruction charge, nor do they report a maximum prison sentence or penalty Tunick could face if convicted. It also remains unclear how the judge will rule on the motion to suppress, or whether the court will ultimately treat the phone wipe as intentional evidence destruction or as an unintended side effect of GrapheneOS's built-in security design.
